abstract: Looped transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared set of transformer layers, offering a parameter-efficient way to scale computation. However, standard residual connections aggregate information across recurrent depth into a single stream, providing limited control over which intermediate representations from preceding layers should be reused. In this paper, we introduce ARLoop, a looped transformer architecture based on attention residuals (Kimi Team, 2026), where the input of each layer is selectively aggregated through attention over model depth. Distinct from standard transformers, we find that looped transformers do not require access to the full residual history: sliding-window depth attention matches or outperforms full-history attention at larger recurrent depths. Across controlled experiments with multiple parameter scales (140M and 370M) and recurrent depths ($R$$=$$1$ to $5$), ARLoop consistently outperforms prior residual designs for looped transformers. More importantly, we further scale ARLoop to 0.6B and 1.2B parameters under a realistic LLM pretraining recipe, demonstrating that the gains transfer to realistic pretraining, with particularly strong improvements on math and coding tasks. Our 1.2B model, pretrained on only 0.5T tokens with three recurrences, outperforms Huginn-3.5B (the only fully-open looped LLM as of our release date) across all evaluated tasks and is competitive with similar-sized non-looped models such as Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data.

sections.body: Looped transformers reuse one set of layers for more depth, but PreNorm residuals add every earlier update with a fixed unit coefficient, so later layers cannot choose which earlier representations to reuse. The paper introduces **ARLoop**, which applies attention over depth so each sublayer weights its residual sources. Controlled runs use 140M and 370M models at recurrence depths R=1 to R=5. The authors also pretrain 0.6B and 1.2B models. ARLoop-0.6B gains +5.2 points on GSM8K and +3.1 points on MBPP over its PreNorm baseline. The section states that sliding-window depth attention is sufficient, which Section 4 tests.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Standard residuals cannot select earlier looped representations, so ARLoop applies attention over depth to each sublayer.

sections.body: This section places looped transformers among universal transformers and recent pretraining work. It names Huginn (3.5B parameters, up to 64 recurrences) and Ouro (1.4B, up to four recurrences), and notes that many looped LLMs release only weights or nothing. It says Huginn is the only release of all training artifacts and reports that PreNorm does not effectively exploit recurrent depth. It claims ARLoop matches or outperforms Parcae, DeepLoop and HyperLoop across budgets in controlled experiments, and that math and code gains are underexplored in prior work.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior looped models release little training detail, and residual designs were rarely tested on math and coding.

sections.body: PreNorm adds each sublayer output with unit weight. ARLoop replaces this with a weighted sum over residual sources, where each weight is a softmax score between a learned query vector for the sublayer and the normalized source. Sublayers are grouped into blocks of S consecutive sublayers, so updates are summed within a block and only block representations are stored. Sliding-window depth attention keeps the input embedding and the W most recent blocks, and it is the default for R>2. This section defines the method only; experimental results appear in Section 4.
sections.heading: ARLoop
sections.headline: Attention residuals weight each earlier residual source, and block grouping with a sliding window cuts the sources each sublayer reads.

sections.body: Models are 140M (6 layers) and 370M (12 layers), pretrained on 11.2B and 29.6B FineWeb-Edu tokens. At 140M, validation perplexity is 18.26 for ARLoop at R=1, 16.38 at R=3 and 15.84 at R=5, against 18.37, 16.91 and 16.34 for PreNormLoop. Table 2 shows sliding-window ARLoopsw at 17.30 versus full-history ARLoopfull at 17.27 for 140M with R=2. At 140M with R=4, the window gives 16.03 against 16.07 for the full history. Full-history attention is used for R≤2 and the window for R>2 in the main setup. The 370M comparison covers only R=1 and R=3, because of computational cost.
sections.heading: Controlled Evaluation of ARLoop
sections.headline: ARLoop gives the lowest validation perplexity among tested residual designs, and sliding windows match full-history attention.

sections.body: The recipe follows SmolLM, using grouped-query attention, SwiGLU, FineWeb-Edu, FineMath and Stack-Edu in a multi-stage schedule with a 4096-token context. Three models are trained: PreNormLoop-0.6B on 180B tokens, ARLoop-0.6B on the same budget, and ARLoop-1.2B on 500B tokens, all with R=3. In Table 3, ARLoop-0.6B scores 40.9 on GSM8K and 36.2 on MBPP, against 35.7 and 33.1 for PreNormLoop-0.6B. ARLoop-1.2B is above Huginn-3.5B on every task and below Ouro on most, which the authors attribute to Ouro's larger data budget. ARLoop-1.2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-2B on all listed benchmarks. Parcae and DeepLoop are not compared at this scale.
sections.heading: Scaling to Practical Pretraining of Looped Transformers
sections.headline: ARLoop-0.6B beats PreNormLoop on seven of eight tasks, and ARLoop-1.2B matches or exceeds Qwen3.5-2B on all eight.

sections.body: Fixed recurrence at R=4 gave better validation perplexity and downstream performance than dynamic-recurrence training at 140M and 370M, so the main experiments use fixed recurrence. Inference-time extrapolation was tested by evaluating beyond the training maximum. Perplexity improves up to the maximum training recurrence but not beyond it. The authors conclude that selective access to earlier representations alone does not enable extrapolation. Training memory is essentially the same as PreNorm. ARLoopfull is approximately 15% slower on average, and the sliding window reduces this gap to approximately 10%.
sections.heading: Further discussion
sections.headline: Fixed recurrence beat dynamic recurrence, and extra recurrences beyond training depth gave no further perplexity gains.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the main results. ARLoop beats PreNorm and prior residual designs in controlled runs. Sliding-window attention matches or beats full history at larger recurrence depths. The gains carry to pretraining, with large math and coding improvements at 0.6B. ARLoop-1.2B outperforms Huginn and is competitive with Qwen3.5-2B despite being trained on substantially less data. The authors summarize that selective residual access helps looped transformers exploit recurrent computation at scale. No new experiments are reported in this section.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Across controlled and pretraining experiments, selective residual access helped looped transformers use recurrent depth.

sections.body:
- Architecture for the 140M and 370M models (Table 5): shared backbone, QK-Norm, ReLU2, RoPE, RMSNorm, and a sliding window of three blocks plus the embedding.
- Value residuals, which the authors say matter for looped models. Without them, Sandwich-Norm training fails, with loss near 7.5.
- Training configuration, learning-rate sweeps, and the evaluation protocol for ten zero-shot tasks.
- Ablation without value residuals (Table 7): PreNorm 18.19, ARLoopfull 17.52, ARLoopsw 18.20, and Sandwich-Norm collapse.
- Per-task results (Table 8), baseline formulas, training cost, and the recurrence extrapolation study.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers architecture, training, value residuals, ablations, per-task results, baseline formulas, and extrapolation details.
